questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
A semester abroad in Japan is a mandatory part of the University of Copenhagen's bachelor's in Japanese studies, and I specifically chose Kanazawa for three primary reasons:

1: Kanazawa is a city with a particularly rich cultural heritage.


2: It was recommended to me by others with previous experience.

3: I figured that a smaller and more quiet city like Kanazawa would personally suit me better than larger cities like Tokyo and Kyoto.

questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are three student different dormitories on campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: My room came equipped with a small kitchen, and there was also one in the common room. Both of them were somewhat Spartan and lacked ovens, but they proved satisfactory in my daily life.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The campus is located about 30 minutes away by bus from the city centre in a somewhat secluded forested mountain area, so perhaps consider other accommodation if that is a potential issue.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The course registration for the first quarter-semester only opened the day before classes started, which made registration a somewhat stressful affair. Syllabuses from past semesters were available, but they only gave an idea of what classes could be available, and you could only see the actual list once registration opened. The registration period continued through the first week of classes, allowing students to deregister from classes after attending orientation and signing up for new ones in their place. It thankfully opened a week beforehand for the second quarter-semester, though.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: An information lecture was held on the day registration opened, and I was able to contact academic advisors for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: It was somewhat burdensome to navigate, but I managed to successfully register for the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try to predict what classes you would like to sign up for as well as possible before the registration period begins.

questions.answer: I took a mix of BA classes in the humanities and social science, and Japanese language courses at beginner-intermediate level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I noticed a comparatively higher focus on classes than self-study. The level of digitalisation varied between classes, but it was overall less than UCPH. All of the written exams were pen and paper only.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you want to study Japanese culture and society while in Japan, then I recommend both the cultural classes and the UNESCO biospheres one. Introduction to Japanese Culture & Thought consists of student presentations on a variety of topics, ending with making a short video about your time at the university and writing a paper about a cultural topic of your choice. Japanese Culture E consists of lectures and a written exam at the end. Both courses granted me fascinating insight into many aspects of Japanese culture, society, and history.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I knew that Japan was a much cheaper country to live in than Denmark, but I was still somewhat surprised by the extent of it. Expenses such as food and rent are much lower than what I'm used to.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Japan has a strong school club culture, and there were clubs for pretty much every common sport and hobby. The international student section also offered bus trips for visiting cultural sites and engaging in activities such as skiing.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Joining a club can be a great way to befriend Japanese students, but potential linguistic and cultural barriers can cause issues. The aforementioned bus trips are fantastic ways to see parts of the country you likely wouldn't visit otherwise, and I highly recommend them.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Kanazawa itself is a culturally rich city with many museums and sights to visit during the week. The Kenroku-en garden and the Omicho Market are personal favourites of mine. Local trains can take you to under-appreciated parts of the Hokuriku region such as the Wakuraonsen spa town, and the city is part of the Shinkansen bullet train network, which allows for easy access to other regions. Kanazawa is located between Kyoto, Osaka, and Tokyo, and I went on weekend trips to all three, which I highly recommend doing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The biggest challenge for me was the language barrier. I had studied Japanese for about a year before coming, but I was still far from fluent. I could navigate everyday situations just fine, but more complex interactions such as dealing with bureaucracy required the use of nonverbal communication and translation tools. The actual culture wasn't that difficult to adjust to, as Denmark and Japan both value order and reservedness.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The Japanese have a reputation for being reserved and difficult to get close to, but it depends on your Japanese language proficiency and social confidence. There are occasionally events to meet new people, and that's a great way to start.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I suppose the language can be called a cultural difference, and it proved a challenge, like I wrote above. I'm a somewhat socially anxious person, and I sometimes missed out on opportunities to interact with locals because I feared embarrassing myself by making mistakes while speaking Japanese. I ended up socialising with other international students more. Partially because I lived in the dormitory for international student students, which naturally made me closer to me, but also because the linguistic barriers simply weren't present.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: i highly appreciated the Japanese dedication to order and efficiency. The services I needed to access were accessible and functioned well, and any communication issues I encountered were quickly resolved through the helpfulness of the people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1: Try to get a good idea of what courses you wish to take beforehand to save yourself trouble during the hectic registration period.

2: Make an effort to quickly establish social connections. Groups form quickly and can be difficult to enter if you try to join later.

3: Knowing at least basic Japanese will go a long way in your everyday life.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not particularly.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To have had the opportunity to experience the society and culture in my everyday life.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Like I have described above, the language barrier proved the greatest challenge.
